title: HTML Elements
summary: An HTML element is one part of a page, such as a heading or a paragraph. Some elements can hold other elements.
introduction: An HTML element is one part of a page, such as a heading or a paragraph. Some elements can hold other elements. A box can hold smaller boxes. HTML parts can fit inside each other too. Learn where each part starts and ends.
learningObjectives: Identify the parts of an element and close tags correctly
Nest elements properly and read the resulting tree
Distinguish empty elements and block versus inline elements

blocks.text:
Tag names are case-insensitive, so `

` works, but the universal convention is lowercase. Use it; mixed case looks careless and makes searching your code harder.
Elements inside other elements must be closed in the reverse order they were opened, like boxes inside boxes. The inner element closes before the outer one.

Overlapping tags like `…` are invalid. Browsers try to repair the damage, but the repaired tree is often not what you intended and CSS or JavaScript then behaves strangely. Close the most recently opened element first.

Because elements nest, every HTML document is a tree. The `<html>` element is the root, `<head>` and `<body>` are its children, and so on. Developer tools show this tree in the Elements panel, and JavaScript calls it the **DOM** (Document Object Model), which you will meet in the [JavaScript DOM](/tutorials/javascript-dom) tutorial.

blocks.title: The tree for a small page
blocks.code:
html
├── head
│   ├── meta
│   └── title
└── body
    ├── h1
    └── p
        └── a

blocks.text:
The rule that matters most: **inline elements should not contain block elements**. A `` may not wrap a `

`, and an `` wrapping a whole `

` is allowed only in modern HTML for linking cards. CSS can change how any element displays, which is covered in the [CSS tutorial](/tutorials/css).

`<div>` (block) and `<span>` (inline) have no meaning of their own; they exist to group content for styling or scripting. They are useful, but reach for a meaningful element first: `<nav>` for navigation, `<article>` for a post, `<button>` for a button. The [semantic elements](/tutorials/html/semantic-elements) lesson covers this in depth.

blocks.title: Validate your HTML
blocks.text: The free [W3C Markup Validation Service](https://validator.w3.org/) reports unclosed tags, bad nesting and misspelled elements. Running it on your pages catches problems browsers silently repair.
